summary: Defines criteria for designing an Autonomous System Border Router that runs BGP4 or IDRP for IP with external routers and OSPF as its internal protocol. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules for a border router that talks one routing language to the outside and another to its own network.

questions: how does bgp interact with ospf
what is an autonomous system border router
what is the ospf external route tag
subtitle: Rules for a border router that speaks BGP4 or IDRP to other networks and OSPF inside its own.

tldr.problem: A router on the edge of an autonomous system must move reachability information between BGP4 or IDRP (outside) and OSPF (inside) without leaking routes, losing path information or creating loops.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets rules for what to export and import, requires the BGP/IDRP identifier to equal the OSPF router ID, encodes path information in the 32-bit OSPF external route tag, and sets how the next hop is filled in.
tldr.outcome: It was a Standards Track document that updated the earlier BGP-3 and OSPF interaction document, and its status is now Historic.

facts.label: Default OSPF metric type on import

today: RFC 1745 was published on the Standards Track but its status is now Historic. It builds on RFC 1654 (BGP-4) and RFC 1583 (OSPF version 2) and replaces the approach of RFC 1403.

sections.title: What an AS Border Router Must Do
sections.content:
This RFC defines criteria for designing an Autonomous System Border Router (ASBR) that runs BGP4 (RFC 1654) or IDRP for IP with ASBRs outside its autonomous system, and OSPF (RFC 1583) as its interior protocol. It says how BGP/IDRP attributes and OSPF fields are set when the two meet: the BGP ORIGIN and AS_PATH (IDRP EXT_INFO and RD_PATH) against the OSPF tag, NEXT_HOP against the OSPF Forwarding Address, and LOCAL_PREF against OSPF cost and type.

Requirement words follow the Host Requirements RFCs. A minimal implementation MUST NOT advertise a route when none of its destinations is reachable via OSPF, MUST merge the PATH into a SET when several exit points in the same AS lead to the same external destination, and MUST set the OSPF tag accurately. The text strongly recommends doing more than the minimum.
sections.plainLanguage: A border router sits between two networks that use different rule books. This paper tells the router how to carry information from one rule book to the other without mixing things up.

sections.title: Exporting and Importing Routes
sections.content:
When exporting OSPF information into BGP/IDRP, the administrator MUST be able to filter selectively by address and mask pair, and by the OSPF tag and its sub-fields. The default MUST be to export nothing. A single setting MUST allow all OSPF inter-area and intra-area pairs to be exported, but external type 1 and type 2 routes MUST NOT be exported unless explicitly configured. Pairs with a non-contiguous mask MUST NOT be exported. The administrator MUST be able to set MULTI_EXIT_DISC statically, and by default it is omitted. There MUST also be a setting for a minimum delay between learning a pair via OSPF and advertising it via BGP/IDRP, with a default of 0.

When importing BGP/IDRP information into OSPF, the default MUST be to import nothing. Implementations SHOULD allow control per destination and per autonomous system. The administrator MUST be able to set the OSPF cost and the metric type, which MUST default to type 2. If LOCAL_PREF is used to build a cost, care is needed, because lower OSPF cost is preferred while higher LOCAL_PREF is preferred. Routes learned from peers inside the same AS MUST NOT be imported, and the ASBR MUST NOT generate a default destination into OSPF unless explicitly configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The router starts out sharing nothing. The network owner has to say exactly which routes may cross the border, and in which direction.

sections.title: Router Identity and Equal-Cost Exits
sections.content:
The BGP/IDRP identifier MUST be the same as the OSPF router ID at all times that the router is up. For IDRP, which does not carry the speaker's identity explicitly, the identifier is bound to the address of the OSPF router ID. This lets an administrator correlate BGP/IDRP and OSPF information.

The more important reason is the case of three ASBRs in one AS. Two of them (RT1 and RT2) can reach an external destination and import it into OSPF, and a third (RT3) advertises it to outside peers. RT3 MUST work out which ASBRs it uses by matching the OSPF router ID of its route with the BGP identifier (or IDRP source address). If it has equal cost routes through both, it MUST merge the PATH through them into a SET. The appendix shows how skipping this can leave a stable forwarding loop between two domains that run OSPF with equal cost multipath routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each border router must use the same name in both of its conversations, so that the router handling the outbound message can tell which exits it is really using.

sections.title: The OSPF External Route Tag
sections.content:
OSPF has a 32-bit external route tag whose meaning is otherwise left to the user. This RFC uses it to set the BGP/IDRP ORIGIN and PATH attributes. The high bit is the Automatic bit. If an administrator sets the tag by hand, it MUST be 0, the tag is just a LocalInfo value, and the route SHOULD be exported with ORIGIN=EGP and PATH=local_AS. This is the default for backward compatibility, and there MUST be a way to enable automatic tag generation.

For automatic tags, the remaining bits are a Complete bit, a 2-bit PathLength, a 12-bit ArbitraryTag and a 16-bit AutonomousSystem number. Six combinations of Complete and PathLength are defined, each with an import rule and an export rule, and PathLength=11 is reserved: routers MUST NOT generate it and ASBRs must ignore such tags.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag is a small sticker on each route. The sticker says where the route came from and how much of its journey is known, so the router can describe it correctly to the outside world.

sections.title: Next Hop and Forwarding Address
sections.content:
Forwarding addresses avoid extra hops between routers that share a network but speak different protocols. In the RFC's example, RT3 and RT4 speak OSPF and RT3 also talks BGP/IDRP with RT1 on a common network.

When RT3 imports a destination from BGP/IDRP into OSPF, it MUST always fill the OSPF Forwarding Address with the BGP/IDRP NEXT_HOP of the destination. When it exports OSPF-internal destinations into BGP/IDRP and all of them are reached through RT4, RT3 MAY set NEXT_HOP to RT4's address, so packets crossing the AS boundary do not take an extra hop through RT3. The RFC likens this to indirect neighbour support in EGP.
sections.plainLanguage: If the shortcut is on the same street, the border router can point visitors straight to it, so they do not have to walk through the border office first.

sections.title: Changes from the BGP-3 Document
sections.content:
Section 6 lists what changed from the earlier BGP 3 and OSPF interaction document, RFC 1403. BGP 4 gives the word route a more complex meaning, and the document now uses "set of reachable destinations" for what RFC 1654 calls NLRI. Reachability exchange now handles variable length net masks, and INTER_AS_METRIC has been renamed MULTI_EXIT_DISC. LOCAL_PREF is now the default metric for importing BGP information into OSPF, instead of a constant.

The old requirement to match an OSPF tag to the BGP identifier could cause loops with equal cost multipath routing. BGP4 fixes this by requiring an ASBR that sees equal cost multipath routes to merge the PATHs into SETs. The BGP identifier must now be an address assigned to the BGP speaker. The document says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: This part lists what was fixed since the older version of the rules, such as a new name for one setting and a better way to avoid routing loops.

viz.caption: AUTOMATIC OSPF EXTERNAL ROUTE TAG (RFC 1745, SECTION 4)

fields.name: Automatic
fields.desc: Set to 1 when an ASBR generated the tag automatically.

fields.name: c
fields.desc: Completeness: set when the ORIGIN of the route is EGP or IGP.

fields.name: pl
fields.desc: Path length the protocol could have carried when the route was imported. 11 is reserved.

fields.name: ArbitraryTag
fields.desc: Defaults to 0 but can be configured.

fields.name: AutonomousSystem
fields.desc: AS number for the destinations; 0 means part of the local AS.
